extracted.intended_audience: business executives and public relations practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and executing public relations/propaganda campaigns for businesses: how to build goodwill, align client and public interests, choose tactics (continuous interpretation vs high-spotting), and manage stakeholder relationships and disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobilize existing psychological motives and group habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and activate familiar psychological motives (esthetic, competitive, gregarious, snobbish, exhibitionist, maternal) and group habits to get people to work for the client for the gratification obtained in the activity itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: soap-sculpturing contests engaged housewives and children by appealing to esthetic and competitive motives and school group activity. Use group leadership/authority to set these motives in concerted motion; design activities people will enjoy for their own sake so they contribute voluntarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use group leadership and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders will lend authority to a campaign only if it touches their own interests; make the campaign appear disinterested or aligned with leaders' aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: distinguished artists/educators sponsored soap competitions because it promoted esthetic cultivation among youth. PR counsel must discover points where client interests coincide with leaders/groups and secure their sponsorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discover and exploit coincidence of interests (enlightened self-interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Find where the client's interests coincide with those of other individuals or groups and develop activities that serve both — creating mutual benefit rather than mere quid pro quo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: railroad assisting chambers of commerce to develop towns (benefits both); bank offering investment services so customers have more to deposit. Emphasize genuine public benefit as part of campaign rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the public thoroughly (structure, prejudices, habits, standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations manager must be familiar with the structure, the prejudices, and the whims of the general public and handle problems with utmost care; you may modify but cannot run counter to public standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implications: understand fashion leaders to change styles incrementally; tailor messages to what the public can understand and accept. Avoid trying to dictate major changes to whole generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize the firm's personality and interpret objectives clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Business must dramatize and express its personality and objectives through every contact point (architecture, cleanliness, employee conduct, exhibits) so the public perceives the firm's character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: bank showing honorable officers, bakery displaying hygienic care, department store using artists for window design. Subtle esthetic suggestion and direct advertising both help dramatize traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous interpretation vs high-spotting (two PR strategies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principal plans: continuous interpretation (control many approaches so public receives desired impression unconsciously) and dramatization by high-spotting (vivid, attention-grabbing events that typify the enterprise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which method or combination is indicated after a full study of objectives and possibilities. Examples of high-spotting: making a building taller than any existing skyscraper; large national radio hook-ups to launch a product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be truthful and avoid exaggerated or false pretenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations must not be a protective coloring to hide real aims; avoid stampeding the public with exaggerated claims or false pretenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad practice: featuring a few high-class items while main stock is cheap (creates a false impression). Good PR interprets the business vividly and truly through every avenue to public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor PR to multiple stakeholder responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize responsibilities to stockholders, dealers, industry, retailers, consumers, employees, and the general public and craft communications/actions appropriate to each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: frequent letters to stockholders encouraging product use; inviting dealers to visit the factory; open factory inspection for consumers; attention to employees' living conditions and president's civic leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify client policy or operations when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: PR counsel may recommend substantive policy changes or trivial execution details (product lines, clerk dress, new branches) to make the business conform to public demand and long-term objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: featuring medium-priced goods to attract future high-end customers; opening a Fifth Avenue branch for prestige; ensuring all aspects, down to doorman politeness, align with intended appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use indirect approaches and target intermediaries when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the PR campaign should be directed not to the ultimate consumers but to intermediaries (railroads, steamship companies, foreign governments, trade partners) whose cooperation benefits the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: luggage manufacturers educating railroads/steamships to ease baggage rules; educating general public on travel clothing to indirectly increase luggage sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage scientific tests, institutional adoption, and opinion leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate product claims via reputable research and pilot programs (hospitals, schools), then publicize favorable results through leaders and institutions to create momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mellon Institute research on gelatine -> use in hospitals and schools -> leaders adopt -> broader adoption follows. Use authoritative endorsements and institutional trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PR to combat unethical or exaggerated advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: When competitors make impossible claims, use PR channels (clinics, schools, professional press) to bring truth to the public and protect honest advertisers' markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: tooth paste competitors making impossible claims; respond through dental clinics, schools, women's clubs, dental press to educate public about real product capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop mutually beneficial public-service or information programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Create services or bureaus (e.g., foot protection bureau, insurance departments, cooking schools, information services) that both serve the public good and promote the product's advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: shoe manufacturer creating foot protection bureau to disseminate accurate foot-care information; baking company suggesting recipes to encourage bread use; gas company maintaining free school of cookery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and avert negative trends in public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey public opinion to discover irreducible opposition and advise actions (explanations or policy modifications) to remove causes of complaint before they escalate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze what aspects are logically explainable vs habitual emotional reactions; recommend modifications sufficient to make readjustment and to prevent demands for government ownership or regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support financial objectives (stock/bond issues, mergers) with PR
rubrics_metrics.description: Public acceptance is critical to successful stock/bond flotations and mergers; PR must build the public's consciousness and confidence in the enterprise to facilitate financing and larger operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Victor Talking Machine Company sold millions in a float because of public acceptance; mergers may succeed or fail depending on acceptance created by expert manipulation of public opinion (not dishonest manipulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain sufficient transparency and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid misleading summaries and concealment (e.g., non-voting shares, brief financial statements) which undermine public confidence; provide enough information for public understanding of a concern's true condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose can lead to distrust and attacks; PR should counsel adequate, truthful disclosure to support long-term goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the changing scale of audiences due to mass production and mass media
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass production requires continuous engagement with a vast and diversified public via advertising and PR to maintain steady demand; reach and methods have changed with large-circulation media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: plan campaigns that account for scale (national broadcasts, millions-reach print) and the need to make customers rather than wait for demand to appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate with trade associations and inter-industry efforts for inter-commodity competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter-commodity and inter-industrial competition often requires cooperative association action rather than single firms acting alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: industries must cooperate to defend against competition from alternative goods; trade associations may conduct collective campaigns to influence public consumption patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spectacle judiciously but account for cost-effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: High-spotting spectacles (celebrity broadcasts, large events) can create enormous attention but raise costs; weigh cost against added value in terms of public perception and product uptake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dodge Victory Six radio hook-up reached an estimated 30 million at high expense; publicists must balance attractiveness of appeal versus cost to the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attempting to dictate the public; aim for give-and-take
rubrics_metrics.description: Business should not expect to dictate to the public; a healthy relationship is reciprocal: business must understand and meet public demands while the public appreciates business benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach communications as a partnership; persuasion must respect public's own standards and willingness to accept changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure PR is an authentic complement to advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations should complement legitimate advertising and help counteract unfair competitive exaggeration by reaching the public through channels other than advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clinics, schools, professional organizations, and press to provide truthful information when advertising is misleading or overly emphatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that every corporate detail can influence public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: No detail is too trivial: employees' homes, factory cleanliness, manager's personal reputation, or philanthropic activities can all affect public attitudes toward the concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR planning must include operational, social, and personal aspects of corporate life; ensure consistency across all public-facing details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ outside PR experts when specialized or indirect approaches are required
rubrics_metrics.description: Businesses often retain outside public relations counsel because correct approaches may be indirect or require specialized knowledge not present in-house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: luggage industry needed to influence railroads and foreign governments — outside experts orchestrated these indirect campaigns effectively.
